items.definition: Lines used to hoist or raise the sails.
Part of the boat between the beam (través) and the stern.
Line attached to the masthead that holds up the boom, so it does not drop onto the deck when the mainsail is lowered.
The widest side part of a boat.
Part of the boat between the bow and the beam.
Port: the left side of the boat when facing the bow.
Starboard: the right side of the boat when facing the bow.
Wire cables running sideways to the masthead that stop the mast moving sideways.
Device used to pull the boom downward.
The tiller: lever that controls the rudder.
Mechanical or electric device (winch) that increases the ability to pull a line.
Space at the back of the boat where the controls are located.
Cross-shaped side strut fixed to the mast that supports the shrouds (spreader).
Fitting fixed to the deck used to secure (belay) lines.
Line used to tension the lower part of the sail's front edge (luff).
Wire cable from the stern to the masthead that prevents the mast from moving forward.
Wire cable from the bow to the masthead that prevents the mast from moving backward.
Device used to tension the stays and shrouds.
Fitting that connects the stays and shrouds to the deck or hull.
Lines that control the sails. Hauling in (caçar) brings the sail toward the centerline; easing (folgar) lets it move away.
Triangular sail set at the bow.
Swivelling joint connecting boom to mast, letting the boom move up, down and side to side.
Wire cable guard (lifeline) running along the edge of the boat.
Rudder: plate-shaped device at the stern used to steer the boat.
Rigging: the set of masts, booms, stays, shrouds and other parts supporting the sails.
Vertical spar that supports the sails and the boom.
Mainsail: the principal sail, set on the main mast.
Blocks (sets of pulleys) that guide lines in a desired direction or form purchases that reduce effort.
Knot: unit of boat speed equal to one nautical mile per hour.
Line used to tension the outer edge (leech, as the source labels it) of the sail.
Foot: unit of length equal to 12 inches.
Stern: the back part of the boat.
Bow: the front part of a boat.
Keel: finlike weight under the hull that resists sideways drift (leeway) and adds stability.
Heeling: tilting the boat toward one side.
Turning the bow away from the wind line; the opposite of heading up.
Sailing with no sails set because the wind is very strong.
Sails set on opposite sides when sailing with the wind from astern (wing and wing).
Port tack: the port side is the side receiving the wind (windward side).
Starboard tack: the starboard side is the side receiving the wind (windward side).
Windward: the direction the wind comes from; opposite of leeward.
Beating: sailing against the wind by making a series of tacks.
Sheeting in: pulling the sheets to tighten the sail.
Tacking: turning the bow through the wind line so the sails change sides.
Gybing: turning the stern through the wind line so the sails change sides.
Head to wind: the bow points straight into the wind, leaving the boat with no headway or steering.
Easing: letting out the sheets.
Close-hauled: sailing as close to the wind line as possible, heading against it.
Close reach: sailing at a point between close-hauled and beam reach.
Heading up: turning the bow toward the wind; the opposite of bearing away.
Luffing: the sail flapping irregularly, from over-easing the sheet or pointing closer to the wind than close-hauled.
Running: sailing with the wind blowing in the same direction the boat is travelling.
Reefing: reducing sail area in strong wind by folding onto the boom (mainsail) or rolling onto the forestay (genoa).
Leeward: the direction the wind is heading toward; opposite of windward.
Beam reach: sailing with the wind perpendicular to the boat's course.

numbers.what: wind angle relative to boat's course

items.definition: Broad reach: sailing at a point between beam reach and running.
True wind: wind speed and direction as measured by a stationary observer.
Apparent wind: wind speed and direction as measured by an observer moving on a boat.
The sail acts like an airfoil, splitting the airflow and deflecting it toward the stern, which drives the boat forward.
Thrust force produced by wind passing along the windward side of the sail.
Effect of air on the leeward side trying to pull away from the sail, creating low pressure behind it and most of upwind power.

numbers.what: share of rig power when sailing upwind

items.definition: Using the venturi effect: the genoa speeds airflow behind the mainsail, lowering pressure further and increasing lift.
Sail trim: sails should be neither over-sheeted nor over-eased; too loose deflects less air, too tight breaks the airflow.

numbers.what: wind angle in over-sheeted example (beam wind)

items.definition: Easing the sheets so air flows on both sides of the sail, used when sails are over-trimmed and push the boat sideways with little forward motion.
The trailing edge of the sail, whose fluttering is used to find the exact trim point when easing sails.
Over-eased sails: the leech flutters, the boat moves slowly with little heel, and the sails need to be trimmed in to fill.
When sailing downwind, set the sails at a right angle to the wind direction.

numbers.what: sail angle to wind direction when sailing downwind

items.definition: Quick rule for sailing upwind: when in doubt, ease the sheets.
Tacking upwind: the only way to reach a destination lying toward the wind, by sailing a series of legs with the bow crossing the wind line.

numbers.what: bow angle to wind line while beating

items.definition: A leg or tack of the zigzag course; changing tack is called giving a bordo.
Tacking manoeuvre: the helmsman warns the crew, turns the tiller, the bow crosses the wind line, sails change sides, and the tiller is centred.
The helmsman, who steers and gives commands to the crew during manoeuvres.
The rudder or tiller in the centre position, set once the sail fills on the new side.
Gybing: changing tack with the wind from astern, as the stern passes through the wind line and the sails change sides.
The boom; when it swings across in a gybe it can do so violently, endangering crew and rigging unless controlled.
The mainsheet: trimmed in just before the gybe and eased just after the boat changes tack to control the boom.
Gybe procedure: from a quartering wind, steer so the stern crosses the wind line, call the warning, trim the mainsail to centre, then readjust after.
Wind coming from the quarter of the boat, the point of sail from which the gybe is begun.
The helmsman's command warning the crew that a gybe is about to be made.
Correct sail trim for the wind angle, which must be kept and readjusted when the wind shifts.
A sudden wind shift that requires the sails to be readjusted; there are two types.
A shift in wind direction, here away from the bow, which over-trims the sails and usually increases heel; harder to diagnose than a shift toward the bow.
Wind indicator that the sailor watches closely to detect wind shifts early.
The amount of sail exposed to the wind, which strongly influences speed, performance and control; strong wind calls for less.
Technique for reducing the mainsail area to suit stronger wind conditions.
Furling device on the forestay used to roll up part of the genoa and reduce its area.
Excessive heeling caused by too much sail area, making the boat unstable and hard to control.
Drag; increases when heel submerges more hull, reducing boat speed.
Sideways drift of the boat, worsened by heel as the keel resists less, hurting upwind performance.
Sailing upwind, the point of sailing whose performance suffers from heel and leeway.
Genoa cars (sheet lead positions), which must be moved forward when the headsail is reduced.
Rule-of-thumb table matching headsail size and type to wind strength: weak, moderate or strong wind.

numbers.what: sail size in strong wind (Storm Jib)

items.term: Tabela simplificada para seleção da vela de proa

items.definition: Small headsail chosen for strong wind in the simplified selection table.
Halyard, the line used to hoist and lower a sail; released to lower the sail and reconnected to the new sail's head.
Head of the genoa, where the halyard connects.
To feed or attach the new sail's luff onto the forestay when changing headsails.
Tack cringle; a new one is set on the luff when reefing and secured at the gooseneck.
Clew cringle; a new one is set on the leech when reefing and secured at the end of the boom.
A reefing point on the mainsail; cruising boats commonly have several, used to reduce sail area.

numbers.what: usual number of reef points on cruising boats

items.definition: The lowest reef point, used as the first step in shortening the sail.
The reef point following the first one, reducing the sail further.
Each reef needs its own dedicated set of lines to secure it.
The new tack corner of the reefed sail, which must be fixed firmly near the gooseneck because it is reinforced to take load.
The new clew corner of the reefed sail, which must be fixed firmly near the boom end because it is reinforced to take load.
Lines holding the excess reefed sail; they are not built to bear load, so tension on them can deform or tear the sail.
The mainsail, which should be kept reasonably flat after reefing to help control the boat.
The sail's camber or shape, adjusted mainly through halyard tension, which affects boat performance.
The luff of the sail; wrinkles along it show whether halyard tension is right.
A full, baggy sail resulting from too little halyard tension.
Wrinkles on the luff or foot that indicate incorrect tension: vertical for too much, perpendicular for too little.
The foot of the mainsail along the boom; same tension principle as the luff, with wrinkles showing wrong tension.
Mainsheet track control; easing it makes the mainsail flatter.
Hanks or luff attachments; headsails without them make luff wrinkles harder to see.
Hoisting and tightening the halyard until the luff looks smooth, which indicates correct tension.
Stronger wind requires more halyard tension to flatten the sail.
Trimming the sheets in; once the wind fills the sail, wrinkles may appear showing more luff tension is needed.
Signs on a waterway, buoys and fixed beacons, that guide traffic and show where it is safe to sail.
Floating markers that form part of the aids to navigation.
Fixed beacons marking a channel, as opposed to floating buoys.
System marking channel sides; returning from sea, red even-numbered marks are on the right and green odd-numbered on the left.
Unlit buoys; red ones have conical tops and green ones flat tops.
Buoys marking channel center where traffic keeps to the right bank, painted with vertical white and red stripes.
Marks used where a channel splits in two; a horizontal red or green stripe on top shows which way the main channel lies.
A green top stripe on a junction mark means the main channel continues to the right.
items.term: Verde, canal principal para a direita

items.definition: A red top stripe on a junction mark means the main channel continues to the left.
items.term: Vermelha, canal principal para a esquerda

items.definition: White and orange buoys marking isolated dangers, not tied to any particular channel.
items.term: bóias especiais pintadas de branco e laranja

items.definition: A life jacket saves energy in the water, helping delay hypothermia; it is advisable for children and those not yet used to the sea's motion.

numbers.what: water temperature in the San Francisco Bay example

items.definition: Dangerous loss of body heat after falling into water, a risk even in tropical waters.
Safety rule: always keep one hand holding a fixed point on the boat, using the other for tasks.
items.term: uma mão para o trabalho no barco e a outra para você

items.definition: Steel wire cables supporting the mast; they can break near the connectors, leaving dangerously sharp ends.
Seasickness, which is common; eased by keeping warm, lying down with head low and keeping the mind occupied.
When nearing a dock, wait until the boat is close enough to step off or on safely rather than jumping.
International collision-avoidance rules deciding which of two boats on a collision course has right of way.
The boat with right of way; it must hold its course so the other skipper can steer clear.
The boat that must give way by manoeuvring to avoid the collision.
Any vessel using an engine for propulsion, including a sailboat under power with sails raised.
Limited ability to manoeuvre; such vessels (large ships in channels, towing, trawling, survey, or in difficulty) get right of way over sailboats.
A sailboat using its auxiliary engine is treated as a power vessel and gets no sail privilege.
When overtaking, the overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the one being overtaken.
Two vessels approaching head-on should both turn to starboard and pass port side to port side.
For two power vessels on crossing courses, the one with the other on its starboard side... actually the one approaching from the other's starboard has right of way; the other alters course.
Sailing vessels generally have right of way over power vessels, so a sailboat under engine should yield to vessels under sail.
Heading for the rules between sailboats, based on which side the wind comes from (port or starboard tack); details follow in the next part.
items.term: Amuras a Bombordo X Amuras a Boreste

items.definition: The side of the boat the wind comes from; whether two boats are on the same or opposite tacks determines who gives way.
A situation in which two boats' courses will bring them together unless one changes course.
Right of way: the status of the vessel that may hold its course, though it must still act to avoid collision.
Windward versus leeward: when two boats are on the same tack, the leeward boat has right of way.
A ship in a narrow channel with restricted manoeuvrability and draft keeps right of way, even while overtaking.
Keeping a lookout both ahead and astern, since ships usually move faster than sailboats.
items.term: vigia a vante e a ré

items.definition: The right-of-way vessel must manoeuvre to avoid collision if the other boat is not acting appropriately. Having priority is no excuse.
Course changes should be bold and decisive so the other skipper understands your intentions.
items.term: alteração de rumo clara e sem hesitação

items.definition: Compass bearing to another vessel. If it stays constant as boats approach, a collision is imminent.
Blind zone on the leeward side from abeam to the bow, where other boats on opposite tacks may be hidden.
Sailing close to the wind. The genoa blind spot is greatest on this point of sail, and rescue approaches aim to end on it.
A crew member posted on the leeward side as lookout when the genoa obstructs the helmsman's view.
Emergency of a person falling into the water, requiring a practised rescue manoeuvre done correctly the first time.
First step: shout immediately to alert the whole crew so everyone can take their role in the rescue.
Cushions, lifejackets or buoys thrown close to the victim, without hitting them, to keep them afloat and visible.
A crew member is assigned to keep watching the victim so the skipper can focus on handling the boat.
Lowering and securing the genoa on deck if it would be hard to control, helping keep the boat under control.
On larger boats, hoisting the victim aboard using a halyard or similar line.
Main goal of the manoeuvre: position the boat to approach the victim close-hauled so speed can be easily shed.
Pick up the victim from the leeward side after first checking wind direction.
The leeward side usually sits lower to the water, making it easier to get the victim aboard.
Fastest way to return to a person overboard when sailing with wind abeam or forward: sail one boat length, gybe, then head up toward the victim.

numbers.what: distance sailed on original course before gybing

items.definition: Final approach to the victim, easing the sheets to slow down and stop the boat alongside, lowering sails if needed to stop it restarting.
Heading up, steering closer to the wind, used to approach the victim on a close-hauled course.
Tacking, the best way to return to the victim when sailing downwind, giving a direct close-hauled course to the person.

numbers.what: distance sailed on original course with wind on the quarter before tacking

items.definition: Figure-eight recovery manoeuvre for strong wind or unsafe gybing, or with a small crew: cross a perpendicular line, tack, bear away, then head up to the victim.

numbers.what: angle of imaginary line between victim and wind

items.definition: Bearing away, turning away from the wind, used after tacking to resume the earlier sail position with tacks on the opposite side.
Reef knot, used to tie the mainsail when reefing, secure objects to fixed points and join lines.
Round turn with two half hitches, a general-purpose knot for attaching things, mostly fenders to posts and lifelines; holds under movement.
Bowline, called the king of knots; forms a loop at a line's end, secure and easy to untie, used for halyards, sheets and rings.
Figure-eight knot, a stopper knot at the ends of sheets and halyards to keep them from escaping their cars or mast slots.
Clove hitch, used to tie a line to a solid point such as a dock post or the tiller.
Sheet bend, joins two lines of similar diameter.
Double sheet bend, made with an extra turn when joining lines of very different diameters.
Cleat hitch, the correct way to secure a line to a cleat.
